summary: This unit teaches you to use delegated powers correctly in a ministry, agency, statutory body or municipal corporation. You will learn what a delegation is and how to read its limits and conditions, how to check financial limits (including totals and splitting), how to make fair, evidence-based decisions, how to deal with conflicts of interest and pressure, and how to record and report your decisions. You will also learn how delegations are kept up to date, reviewed and controlled.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. In a public body, the law or the head of the organisation gives certain **powers**: to spend money, sign contracts, grant licences, approve leave, hire staff, pay claims. One person cannot use all of them, so the powers are passed down in writing to officers who can use them at the right level. A passed-down power is a **delegation**. This unit is about using delegations **correctly**: within their limits, with fair decisions, with honesty and with a proper record.

An officer who uses a delegation wrongly can cause a decision to be invalid, harm a member of the public, waste public money, and damage her own career and the body's reputation. An officer who uses it well helps the body to decide quickly and fairly at the right level.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the office
rows: Understand delegations
Explain what a delegation is, who gives and holds it, why it is used and who stays accountable.
Read an instrument of delegation
Find the power, its limits, its conditions and who may act; know what is and is not covered.
Check limits and totals
Test every request against transaction and cumulative limits and against the total value of the commitment; never split to avoid a limit.
Make sound decisions
Use relevant evidence, serve the proper purpose, keep an open mind, give a fair hearing and decide on time.
Manage conflicts and pressure
Declare interests, step aside, refuse gifts and resist improper instructions.
Record and report
Keep a full file note of each decision, report as required and explain how to seek a review.
Deal with sub-delegation and acting
Know when a power may be passed on or used by an acting officer.
Maintain the framework
Keep the register current, monitor use, correct errors and revise delegations after changes.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with workplace scenarios, many with sums, on limits, conditions, decision-making, conflicts of interest and records.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and calculations) and longer answers on decision steps, principles, conflicts and setting up a framework.

**Practical group tasks**: deciding applications from a case pack against an instrument of delegation and recording the decisions; and reviewing a delegations register after a restructure and briefing managers on a revised instrument.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact terms: delegate, delegator, instrument of delegation, sub-delegation, procedural fairness or natural justice, conflict of interest, revocation, ultra vires, register, statement of reasons, accountability and acting officer. Learn them from the key terms in the Revision section.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: This unit describes the general principles. Do not quote sections of any law: your body's own instrument, its HR and finance policies and its legal unit tell you what applies. When you are unsure whether a power is covered, ask before you decide.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **delegation** is a formal grant of power to act for the holder of that power. The person or body that gives it is the **delegator**. The officer who receives it is the **delegate**. The power must come from a law, a regulation or the head of the body, and it can be passed on only as far as the law or the instrument allows.

head: Point
A delegation
Simply assigning a task
rows: What is passed on
The **power to decide** and to bind the organisation (to approve, sign, refuse, spend)
The work to be done
Form
A written instrument of delegation
An instruction, which may be spoken
Example
The Director, Finance, may approve purchases up to a stated amount
An officer is asked to prepare the purchase order for the director to sign
If something goes wrong
The decision may be invalid if it is outside the delegation
The decision-maker is still the person who holds the power

ul: Decisions are made **at the right level, promptly**, close to the facts and the public.
Senior officers are freed for planning and policy.
Officers develop their skills and take ownership.
Services are quicker: a customer does not wait for the head of the agency to sign every permit or leave form.

blocks.p: Delegating a power does not remove the delegator's responsibility. The head of the body, usually the Permanent Secretary or chief executive (the **accounting officer** for the money), stays **accountable overall**, together with the director or officer who uses the power. A delegate is accountable to the delegator for how she uses the power and is answerable in her own right for decisions she makes. **Accountability** means being answerable for your decisions and their results.
The **instrument of delegation** is the formal written document that grants the delegation and sets out its limits and conditions. It should say:

ul: **Who** delegates and **who** receives the power (usually by **post**, such as "Director, Finance", not by name);
**What** power is delegated, and under which law or policy;
the **limits**: amounts per transaction, totals over a period, types of decisions;
the **conditions**: for example "subject to available budget", "in consultation with the Finance Director", "in accordance with the procurement rules";
whether the power may be **sub-delegated**, and whether it passes to an **acting** officer;
the **date** it starts, any end date, and the **reporting** required.

blocks.note: Delegations are usually made to a **position**, not a named person, so that the power continues when the person in the post changes. A new officer in the post uses it from the day she is properly appointed. A person who leaves the post loses it at once.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Why a delegation must be in writing

blocks.p: A written delegation makes its **scope and limits clear and provable**. If a decision is challenged, by an auditor, a court or a member of the public, the body must be able to show that the officer had the power. A spoken delegation, or a message that says only "go ahead", is easily disputed and does not protect the officer.

Most bodies keep a **register**: an official list of all current delegations, who holds each one and its limits. The register is kept up to date, is available to officers who need it, and is checked whenever posts, laws or limits change.

blocks.note: In Jamaica the powers of a ministry or a public body come from legislation and from the financial and procurement rules for the public sector. The head of the organisation (for a ministry, the Permanent Secretary as accounting officer) delegates in writing. Municipal corporations are led by the Mayor and the corporation's chief executive. Always use the instrument and rules of your own body.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: **Identify** the power you are being asked to use
**Find** it in your instrument of delegation: is it listed?
**Check each limit**: this transaction, the total this quarter or year, and the total value of the whole commitment
**Check each condition**: budget, procurement rules, consultation, approvals
**Decide**: within the delegation and all conditions met, you may decide; otherwise **refer** it to the officer who holds the power
**Record** what you checked and what you decided

blocks.p: Financial delegations normally have two kinds of limit:

head: Limit
What it means
Example
rows: **Per transaction** (single commitment)
The largest amount you may approve at one time
"Up to J$800,000 for any one purchase"
**Cumulative** (total over a period)
The largest total you may approve in a quarter or year
"J$3,000,000 in total each quarter"

blocks.p: A request must be **within both limits**. A request that is below the per-transaction limit still has to be referred if it would take the total for the quarter above the cumulative limit.
**Worked example.** Mr Lewis may approve J$800,000 per transaction and J$3,000,000 in total each quarter. So far this quarter he has approved J$2,150,000.

ul: A request for J$600,000 is below J$800,000 and below J$850,000: within both limits.
A request for J$900,000 is above the J$800,000 transaction limit and above the J$850,000 room left: **refer it**.

blocks.p: Compare the limit with the **whole value** of what the body is committing to, not only the first payment or the annual amount.

ul: A cleaning contract of J$450,000 a year for three years has a total value of 3 × 450,000 = **J$1,350,000**. If the delegate's limit is J$1,000,000, she must refer it.
A security contract for 2 years at J$75,000 a month: 24 × 75,000 = J$1,800,000.
A contract that "may be renewed" or has options should be valued with the options, as the policy says.

blocks.p: **Splitting** means dividing one need into several smaller orders so that each falls under the limit. It is **improper**, even if the money is available. If you must buy J$1,200,000 of equipment and your transaction limit is J$800,000, you may not order it as two items of J$600,000. The need, taken as a whole, is above your limit and must be referred. Auditors look for several purchases from the same supplier in the same week, just under the limit.

Words such as **"subject to available budget and the overtime policy"** mean that **both** must be met. Having the power does not mean the budget exists or the policy permits the action. Other common conditions:

head: Condition
What you must do
rows: "Subject to available budget"
Check the commitment control or budget report: is there an unspent, correctly coded allocation?
"In accordance with the procurement rules"
Follow the public-sector procurement rules: quotations or bids for the value, approved suppliers, record of evaluation
"In consultation with the Finance Director"
Consult and record that you did; a decision made without it is outside the delegation
"With the prior approval of ..."
Obtain the approval **before** you decide, not afterwards
"Within the approved plan"
Check the activity is in the approved work plan or budget

blocks.note: A decision outside the delegation, or without a required condition, may be **invalid** (the Latin term is **ultra vires**, meaning beyond the powers) and may have to be referred up, reversed or ratified by someone who holds the power. A genuine supplier or member of the public acting in good faith can be harmed, which is why the officer must check first.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: If you are not sure whether your delegation covers a decision, such as waiving a late-payment fee, **get advice before you decide**: ask your director, HR, finance or the legal unit. It is much easier to ask first than to correct a wrong decision later.

head: Situation
The rule
rows: **Sub-delegation** (passing the power on to someone else)
A delegate may sub-delegate **only if the instrument allows it**, usually to a named post and within her own limits. She should not simply tell her assistant to "sign for me".
**Acting officer**
Someone formally appointed to act in a post may use that post's delegations **only if the instrument covers whoever acts** in the post. The appointment is in writing, with dates.
**The delegator**
The head of the body usually **may still use the power himself**, unless the law says otherwise: delegating does not give the power away.
**Revocation or variation**
The delegator may vary or revoke (cancel) a delegation, for instance if conditions are repeatedly ignored.

blocks.p: Both sub-delegation and acting arrangements add risk, because the person using the power may be less experienced, or the register may be out of date. Controls include a written appointment, a short list of what is covered, extra monitoring and a return to normal when the absence ends.

flow: **Receive** the matter and check it is in time and complete
**Check the power**: is this decision in your instrument, and within your limits and conditions?
**Check for a conflict of interest** and decide whether you must step aside
**Gather the facts and evidence**; ask for missing information; hear the affected person where the decision may harm him
**Apply the law, policy and criteria** that the delegation requires, and weigh the facts of this case
**Decide** within the time set by the service standard
**Record** the power used, the facts, the reasons and the date
**Tell** the person the decision and reasons, and how to seek a review or appeal

head: Principle
What it means
Public-sector example
rows: **Act within power**
Use only the power you hold, and meet its conditions
A clerk may not approve a payment above her limit
**Take relevant matters into account, and only those**
Consider what the law and policy make relevant; ignore irrelevant matters
A vendor's licence is refused because he once complained about the unit: the complaint is not relevant to the licence criteria
**Use the power for its proper purpose**
Use it for the reason it was given, not to punish or reward
A transfer used mainly to punish an officer for a disagreement breaches this principle
**Use judgement; do not fetter your discretion**
Weigh the facts of each case. Guidelines help, but do not refuse every application of one type without looking at the facts
Refusing every hardship grant to people over sixty because of an unwritten unit rule
**Be unbiased**
Decide with an open mind, free from personal interest and prejudice
An officer decides her brother-in-law's tender: she must step aside
**Give a fair hearing (procedural fairness)**
The person must know the concerns and have a fair chance to reply before a harmful decision
Before cancelling a vendor's licence, tell him the concerns and hear his reply
**Base the decision on evidence**
Relevant, reliable evidence on the file, not rumour or pressure
A refusal rests on inspection reports, not on gossip
**Give reasons**
Explain how the decision was reached
A refusal letter states the criteria and why they were not met
**Decide on time**
Delay can harm people and public trust; follow service standards
Applications are decided within the time published in the service standards

blocks.p: **Procedural fairness** (also called **natural justice**) is the duty to hear a person and to act without bias before making a decision that affects them. It has two main parts: the person must **know the case against him** and have **a fair chance to reply**, and the decision-maker must be **unbiased**.

Policies and guidelines help officers decide consistently. A delegate should **follow them**, but should still **weigh the facts of each case**. If two officers with the same delegation decide similar grant cases very differently, the remedy is better guidance, training and peer review of cases, not a rule that ignores the facts.

ul: If a senior politician, a friend or a manager phones to tell you how to decide a matter that is yours to decide, **decide it yourself, on the merits**, and write a note of the call. Accepting an instruction on a decision that the law gives to you is a failure to use your own judgement.
If you are given an instruction that is outside your delegation, or against the rules, say so politely and refer it or ask for it in writing.
You may seek **advice**, for example from the legal unit, but **you** make the decision, after weighing the advice.

blocks.p: Applications often contain medical reports, income details and addresses. Use such information **only for the decision**, keep it secure, and share it only with those who need it. The general purpose of the data protection law is to say what may be collected, why, and how it is kept safe.

blocks.h: Hearing a person before a harmful decision

blocks.p: Suppose a corporation officer is considering cancelling a food vendor's licence after reports of unsafe practices. Procedural fairness means she should:

flow: Check that the licence conditions and the delegation allow cancellation
Gather the evidence, such as inspection reports, and check that it is reliable
Write to the vendor stating the concerns and the evidence, with a reasonable time to reply
Consider his reply and any new evidence with an open mind
Decide, record the reasons and tell him in writing, with how to ask for a review
Act at once, if there is serious risk to public health, under the emergency or interim powers the law gives, and then complete the fair process

blocks.p: A **conflict of interest** is a situation in which an officer's private interests could improperly influence an official decision, or appear to. The interest may be financial, a family or friendship link, a business role, a past or planned job, or a personal grudge. It exists even if the officer believes she can be fair. **The appearance of bias can be as harmful as bias.**

flow: **Recognise** it: ask "Could someone reasonably think my interest affects this decision?"
**Declare** it in writing to your supervisor or the person the policy names, **before** you do anything on the matter
**Step aside**: take no part in the discussion, the evaluation or the decision
**Make sure** another suitably authorised officer decides
**Record** the declaration and who decided instead

head: Situation
Right response
rows: A tender includes a company owned by your brother-in-law
Declare it and step aside from the evaluation and the decision
You are a director of one of the companies bidding for a housing project
Declare the interest, take no part in the choice of partner or contractor
You must approve your own overtime claim
Have **another authorised officer** approve it; nobody approves a claim in their own favour
A grant applicant is your cousin's community group
Declare it; another officer decides the application
An applicant offers you a gift basket while his application is pending
**Decline it** and record the offer, as policy requires. Gifts and favours from people who want decisions are never accepted

ul: Follow your body's gift and hospitality policy.
Refuse anything offered by someone who has a matter before you, or may have one soon.
Record all offers, accepted or refused.
Never ask for anything for yourself or for a friend because of your position.

blocks.h: Integrity in using a delegated power

blocks.p: The conduct that best shows integrity is **acting openly, fairly and within limits**: declaring interests, deciding on merit, keeping records, using public money as if it were your own and being willing to explain your decisions. Public bodies are also subject to anti-corruption and integrity rules in Jamaica; refer to the body's policy and the oversight bodies' guidance.

blocks.note: If you believe you have been offered a bribe, or you are asked to approve something improper, do not argue or accept: refuse, write down what happened and report it at once to your supervisor or the officer named in your body's reporting policy.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Records, reporting, review and correcting errors

blocks.p: The file must show how the decision was made. A good record contains:

head: Item
Example
rows: The **power used**
"Instrument of delegation, item 4: approval of purchases up to J$800,000"
The **facts and evidence**
The application, quotations, inspection report, budget check
The **reasons**
Why the criteria were or were not met; why a particular quotation was chosen
**Conflicts declared**
Any declaration and who decided instead
The **decision and date**
Approved / refused / referred; date; officer's name and post
**Notification**
When and how the person was told, and how he may seek a review

blocks.p: Why reasons matter: they let the person and any reviewer see **how** the decision was made, they discipline the decision-maker, and they allow errors to be corrected. A one-word email, "Approved", with no reference to authority, makes it hard to show that the decision was authorised.

blocks.note: What is not on the file may as well not have happened. Write the record **when** you decide, not months later when it is questioned.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Many bodies require delegates to report **monthly** (or quarterly) the decisions made under financial delegations, so the delegator can **monitor** how the power is used.

The reviewer compares each approval with the delegate's limits and conditions. If a monthly report shows that an officer with a J$500,000 limit approved 14 payments and one was J$620,000, the reviewer should **look into the one that broke the limit**, not ignore it because 13 of 14 were fine.
The delegator can review **samples** of decisions and files, check trends and ask for explanations.
Review results feed back into guidance and training.

blocks.p: A person who is not happy with a delegate's decision, such as a refused permit, should be told **how to seek a review or appeal**: to whom, in what form and by when. A body that offers a review corrects its own mistakes and keeps public trust.

**Worked example.** A delegate made 24 decisions last year and 3 were changed on review. 3 ÷ 24 × 100 = **12.5%** changed. A high figure points to training, guidance or a quality problem, and should be investigated.

blocks.h: If you find that you made an error

blocks.p: Suppose an officer realises that two weeks ago she approved a payment above her delegated limit. She should:

flow: **Stop** and do not approve anything further of the same kind
**Tell** her supervisor or the delegator promptly: do not hide it or wait for an audit
**Check** the facts: the amount, the limit, the condition missed, the status of the payment
**Agree remedies** with the person who holds the power: ratify the decision if the law allows, correct, stop or recover the payment
**Record** what happened and what was done
**Learn**: find the cause (unclear limit, no check, pressure) and fix it

blocks.note: Honest, early reporting of an error is treated far more kindly than an error that is hidden and then discovered. An officer who hides a mistake adds a breach of integrity to the original error.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Setting up and keeping a sound framework

blocks.p: The head of a public body, and each director who delegates, is responsible for a **framework** that makes delegation safe.

head: Element
What good practice looks like
rows: **Written instrument**
Clear, to positions, listing powers, limits, conditions, sub-delegation and acting rules
**Register**
One current list, easy to find, with dates; updated whenever the instrument changes
**Training**
Officers who receive delegations are trained in the powers, decision rules, conflicts of interest and records before they use them
**Guidance and checklists**
Short guides and standard decision forms
**Monitoring**
Reports, sample checks and internal audit; follow-up of exceptions
**Review**
Regular review of limits and powers; review after any restructure or change in law; quick revocation or variation where needed
**Emergency arrangements**
A written emergency procedure, such as during a hurricane, with limits, approvals and records

ul: If the head of an agency **restructures** divisions and renames posts, the **register and instrument must be reviewed and updated** to match the new posts. Otherwise powers belong to posts that no longer exist, or nobody holds powers that are needed.
If a **new law** or policy changes the conditions for a permit or payment, **update the delegations and guidance, and brief staff before** delegates apply the new rules.
If a delegate repeatedly ignores conditions, the delegator **varies or revokes** the delegation, retrains and monitors more closely.

blocks.p: During a hurricane, a parish disaster office may need to buy supplies that cost more than an officer's limit. The officer should use the **emergency procedure** set out by the body, or **refer to the officer who holds the power**, by phone if necessary, and note it down at once. Emergencies do not suspend the rules: they are the reason bodies write emergency rules in advance.

A delegation to approve purchases does not replace the **procurement rules for public bodies**. Those rules say how many quotations or what kind of bid is needed at each value, how suppliers are chosen, and how decisions are recorded. A delegate must follow both.

A newly promoted officer who has received several delegations is best prepared by **training on the powers and the decision rules**. Officers who apply the same delegation differently are helped by guidance, case discussion and peer review.

blocks.note: Check your body's current instrument, register and policies. Names of posts, limits and procedures change often, and the register is the only authority for what you may do today.
blocks.label: Jamaica

terms: Delegation
A formal grant of power to act for the holder of that power
Delegator
The person or body that gives a delegation
Delegate
The officer who receives and uses a delegated power
Instrument of delegation
The formal written document that grants a delegation and sets out its limits and conditions
Register
The official list of all current delegations, holders and limits
Transaction limit
The most a delegate may approve in a single commitment
Cumulative limit
The most a delegate may approve in total over a period such as a quarter
Splitting
Dividing one need into smaller orders to stay under a limit; improper
Sub-delegation
A delegate passing a delegated power on to another officer
Acting officer
Someone formally appointed to fill a post temporarily, who may use its delegations if the instrument allows
Revocation
The formal cancelling of a delegation by the delegator
Ultra vires
Latin for "beyond the powers": a decision made outside legal authority
Procedural fairness (natural justice)
The duty to hear a person and to act without bias before deciding something that affects them
Conflict of interest
A situation in which private interests could improperly influence an official decision
Statement of reasons
A written explanation of the facts, evidence and reasoning behind a decision
Accountability
Being answerable for your decisions and their results
Accounting officer
The head of a ministry or body who is answerable for its funds; delegates financial powers in writing

c1.title: Purchases at a ministry's regional office in Mandeville
c1.text: Mr Anthony Lewis is Regional Director at a ministry's office in Mandeville. His written delegation lets him approve purchases up to J$800,000 per transaction and J$3,000,000 in total each quarter, "subject to available budget and the procurement rules". This quarter he has already approved J$2,150,000. Three requests are on his desk: A, J$600,000 to repair the generator; B, J$900,000 for vehicle tyres and batteries; C, J$200,000 for office furniture. The budget report shows enough budget for all three. A supplier has offered to send two separate invoices of J$450,000 for request B.

c2.title: A vendor's licence at a municipal corporation in St James
c2.text: Ms Pauline Reid is the licensing officer at a municipal corporation in St James. Under her delegation she decides applications and cancellations for market vendors' licences. An inspector's report says that a vendor, Mr Foster, sold meat without refrigeration on three days. A rival vendor has also told Ms Reid that Mr Foster "supports the wrong political party". Ms Reid is considering cancelling his licence. The corporation's policy requires officers to give reasons and say how to ask for a review.

c3.title: Small grants at a ministry in Kingston
c3.text: Mr Dwight Palmer is a programme officer in a ministry in Kingston. His delegation lets him approve community grants of up to J$500,000 "in consultation with the Finance Director". Two applications are before him. Group X is run by his cousin. Group Y asks for J$450,000 and meets all the criteria, but Mr Palmer is thinking of approving it without contacting the Finance Director because she is on leave until next month and the group wants an answer this week.

c4.title: Absence of a director at a statutory body
c4.text: Mrs Joy Campbell is Director of Corporate Services at a statutory body in Spanish Town and holds delegations to approve contracts up to J$2,500,000. She will be on leave for six weeks. She wants her secretary to "sign for her" while she is away, and she has told Mr Ricardo Bailey, the Finance Manager, by phone that he can "look after things". The instrument says the delegation passes to "the officer formally appointed to act in the post" and says nothing about sub-delegation. The chief executive of the body is in the building.

c5.title: After a restructure at a government agency
c5.text: A government agency in St Catherine merged two divisions and renamed several posts six months ago. Its register of delegations still lists people by name, including two officers who have left. An audit has found that an officer whose limit is J$500,000 approved a J$620,000 payment last month, and that no one at the agency has reviewed any monthly reports since the merger. The new head of the agency wants to put things right. Last year the agency's delegates made 40 decisions that were reviewed, and 6 were changed.

questions.q: How much more may Mr Lewis approve this quarter under his cumulative limit?
questions.why: Quarterly limit J$3,000,000 minus J$2,150,000 already approved leaves J$850,000. J$800,000 is only the per-transaction limit, and J$2,150,000 is the amount already approved.

questions.q: Which of the three requests may Mr Lewis approve himself, if the conditions are met?
o: A and C, as together they total J$800,000, within the J$850,000 left
A, B and C, because the budget report shows funds for all three
B only, because it is the largest request and has the most budget
A only, because C would take the total over the quarterly limit for the period
questions.why: A (J$600,000) and C (J$200,000) are each under the transaction limit, and together they total J$800,000, within the J$850,000 left. B (J$900,000) is over the J$800,000 limit and must be referred.

questions.q: Why can Mr Lewis not accept the supplier's offer of two invoices of J$450,000 for request B?
o: Two invoices from one supplier would double the delivery charge to the ministry office
Each invoice would have to be approved by a different officer in the region
A supplier may send only one invoice for each purchase order the ministry issues
Splitting one purchase to stay under the limit is improper; it must be referred
questions.why: The need is one purchase worth J$900,000, which is above his J$800,000 limit. Dividing it to fit under the limit is splitting, which the delegation does not allow.

questions.q: The delegation says 'subject to available budget and the procurement rules'. What does this mean for request A?
o: He may approve if the budget is available, and the procurement rules apply only above J$800,000
He may approve only if the budget is available and the correct procurement steps have been followed
He may approve because the amount is within his limit, and the conditions are for the finance unit
He may approve if either the budget or the procurement condition is met, but not both
questions.why: 'Subject to' conditions must all be met. A limit gives the power; the conditions decide whether it can be used for this purchase.

questions.q: What should Ms Reid do before deciding whether to cancel Mr Foster's licence?
o: Cancel the licence at once, because the inspection report is clear
Tell him the concerns and the evidence, and give him a fair chance to reply
Ask the rival vendor to confirm his complaint and send it to Mr Foster
Wait for another inspection and decide without telling Mr Foster of the first
questions.why: Procedural fairness means the person affected knows the case against him and may reply before a decision that harms him is made.

questions.q: How should Ms Reid treat the rival's comment about Mr Foster's political party?
o: Record it as part of the evidence and weigh it with the inspection report
Pass it to the Mayor so that he can decide how much weight it deserves
Use it only if Mr Foster's replies to the inspection report are not satisfactory
Ignore it, because it is not a relevant matter under the licence criteria
questions.why: A decision-maker must consider relevant matters and ignore irrelevant ones. Political opinion has no place in decisions about food safety and licence conditions.

questions.q: Which information must Ms Reid's file record if she decides to cancel the licence?
o: The power used, the facts and evidence, her reasons and the date
The decision, the date and the rival vendor's explanation of events
The decision and the amount of fees that Mr Foster has paid to date
The decision, her reasons and the political views of those involved
questions.why: A record shows the power used, the facts, the reasons and the date, so reviewers can see how the decision was made. A reviewer cannot rely on gossip or fees.

questions.q: After the decision, what should Ms Reid tell Mr Foster?
o: The decision only, since the reasons are for the corporation's file
The decision and the name of the vendor who made the complaint
The decision and her reasons, and how he can ask for a review
The decision and that it is final and cannot be reviewed
questions.why: Fair practice is to give the decision with reasons and tell the person how to seek a review or appeal.

questions.q: Group X is run by Mr Palmer's cousin. What should he do?
o: Decide the application himself, since his cousin will not receive any special treatment
Refuse the application, so that nobody can say that he favoured his family
Approve it only if the group's score is the highest of all the applicants
Declare the interest in writing and have another authorised officer decide the application
questions.why: A conflict of interest must be declared and the officer must take no part. Refusing his own relative's application is still taking part in a decision on it.

questions.q: Mr Palmer wants to approve Group Y without contacting the Finance Director. What is the problem?
o: Grants of J$450,000 are above his limit, so he must refer all of them to the Finance Director
'In consultation with' is a condition of his delegation, so deciding without it is outside it
The Finance Director must approve every application, whatever the delegation says
There is no problem, because the group meets the criteria and has waited a long time
questions.why: The consultation is part of the delegation. Meeting the criteria is not enough: if the condition is not met, the decision may be invalid. He should consult the acting Finance Director or whoever the instrument allows.

questions.q: Group Y's decision must also be recorded. What should the file show about the consultation?
o: Only the decision, as consultation does not belong on the file
The name of the Finance Director, who must sign the final decision
Who was consulted, when and what was said, with the reasons for the decision
The date, as the content of the consultation is private between the officers
questions.why: The file should show that the condition was met: who was consulted and when. Without a record it is hard to prove the decision was within the delegation.

questions.q: If the Finance Director is on leave, what is the right way to meet the condition?
o: Consult the officer formally acting in her post, if the instrument allows, or refer it
Ask any colleague in the finance unit who is willing to take the call on her behalf
Wait until she returns, even if the group is left without any answer for a month
Consult her by text during her leave, and record only that he tried to reach her
questions.why: An acting officer who is formally appointed may be consulted if the instrument covers the person acting in the post. Otherwise refer the matter to someone who holds the power.

questions.q: Mrs Campbell wants her secretary to 'sign for her'. What should she do?
o: Not do it: sub-delegation needs the instrument's permission, and this instrument is silent
Let the secretary sign, but keep a log of every contract she signs while Mrs Campbell is away
Let the secretary sign contracts up to J$1,000,000, which is less than Mrs Campbell's own limit
Let the secretary sign if she has a letter from Mrs Campbell, written before the leave begins
questions.why: A delegate may pass on her power only if the instrument permits sub-delegation. Where it is silent, she cannot, and a signature by someone without power may be invalid.

questions.q: What is needed so that Mr Bailey may use Mrs Campbell's delegation while she is away?
o: A phone call from Mrs Campbell to the finance staff to say he is in charge
A note from Mrs Campbell to the secretary asking her to inform the suppliers
A written appointment to act in the post, covering the dates of her leave
The agreement of the staff in the department that he should take charge
questions.why: The instrument passes the delegation to the officer formally appointed to act. A formal, written appointment with dates is the proof that he has the power.

questions.q: While Mrs Campbell is away, may the chief executive still use the power to approve contracts?
o: No, because the power has passed to the acting officer and two people cannot hold it together
Usually yes, as delegating does not remove the delegator's own power, unless the law says otherwise
Yes, but only if Mr Bailey agrees in writing before the chief executive signs anything
No, because a power that has been delegated can then be used by the delegate only
questions.why: A delegator keeps the power. Delegation shares it with a delegate, but the delegator usually remains able to use it, subject to the law and the instrument.

questions.q: Mrs Campbell returns from leave. What happens to Mr Bailey's use of the delegation?
o: It continues until the chief executive withdraws it, in writing, some time later
It continues, as he has used it well and the staff are now used to him as acting head
It ends only when he has completed every contract that he has started
It ends with the appointment period; contracts he properly approved stay valid
questions.why: An acting appointment covers set dates. When it ends, so does his use of the power; decisions made properly while he held it remain valid.

questions.q: Two managers in the merged division each say the other holds the power to approve overtime. What does this most likely show?
o: Both managers hold the power and may use it jointly, as the law provides
The instrument and register do not clearly give the power to a post
The power has lapsed, so the head of the agency alone may approve overtime
One manager is not following the policy and must be disciplined at once
questions.why: Unclear, outdated delegations after a restructure leave people unsure who may decide. The instrument and register should name the post that holds each power.

questions.q: What should happen about the officer who approved J$620,000 against a limit of J$500,000?
o: Investigate, tell the delegator and agree whether to ratify, correct or recover the payment
Treat it as a small error, because all of the other approvals were within her limit
Dismiss her at once, because exceeding a limit is always gross misconduct by an officer
Ask her to approve a second payment for the difference, so that the books will balance
questions.why: An approval over the limit needs investigation, not instant punishment or concealment. The delegator and finance decide on ratification or recovery, and the controls are fixed.

questions.q: Which control would best help the agency to find over-limit approvals earlier in future?
o: An annual reminder to all officers to keep within the limits of their delegations
A rule that every payment above J$100,000 must have two signatures, whatever the delegation
A rule that officers hold their limits only until the next audit has been done
Monthly reports of decisions, checked against each officer's limits by the delegator's office
questions.why: Regular reports checked against the register let the delegator spot a breach within weeks. A reminder alone does not check anything.

questions.q: Last year 6 of the agency's 40 reviewed decisions were changed. What percentage was this, and what does it suggest?
o: 15%, which shows that the review system is too strict and should be reduced
6%, which is low enough that no action is needed
15%, which suggests that delegates may need guidance or training
6%, which shows that most delegates are using their powers wisely
questions.why: 6 ÷ 40 × 100 = 15%. A rate this high is a sign that delegates may need clearer guidance, training or peer review.
